title: Elders for Crete, and Teachers to Silence
sum: The letter opens with a long greeting. Paul calls himself a slave of God and an apostle, sent for the faith of God's chosen ones and for the truth that goes with godliness, all resting on the hope of eternal life promised by "the God who does not lie." He greets Titus as his "true-born child" in a faith they share, though Paul was a Jew and Titus a Greek.

Then the task: Titus was left on Crete to put the churches in order and appoint elders in each town. The elder, or overseer, must be beyond accusation in his marriage, his children, his temper, his drinking and his money, welcoming to strangers and firm in sound teaching. The reason follows at once: many on the island, "especially those from the circumcision", are upsetting whole households for money. A Cretan poet's line, "Cretans are always liars", is turned against them. To the clean all things are clean; the opponents claim to know God, but their actions deny him.
readings: Verses 5-9 read like a list of qualifications for office, and churches have used them that way ever since. Read this way, the chapter sets standards that every church still applies when it chooses leaders.
Read as an answer to a crisis

The list is framed by the opponents (1:10-16). Each quality of the elder answers a fault of the false teachers: they are greedy, he is not; they are unruly, his children are not; they deny God by their works, he loves what is good. Read this way, the list is less a timeless form than a portrait of the opposite of the troublemakers on Crete.

views.H: Crete was a large, mountainous island with many towns and a Jewish population (Philo, Embassy to Gaius 282, names Crete among the islands with Jewish communities; Acts 2:11 has Cretans at Pentecost). Acts shows Paul only sailing past it as a prisoner (Acts 27:7-21), so this mission, if historical, falls outside Acts. The churches met in homes, which is why the teachers could "turn whole households upside down". Tradition, recorded by Eusebius (Church History 3.4.6), made Titus the first overseer of the churches of Crete.
views.C: For most critical scholars the chapter reflects a church a generation or more after Paul, organizing itself with settled leaders and a fixed body of "sound teaching" to guard; the journey to Crete is part of the letter's setting rather than a report. Defenders of Paul answer that a new mission on a large island would need exactly such instructions, and that "elders" were already appointed in Paul's churches (Acts 14:23). The arguments are on the topic page The Pastoral Letters.
views.L: The greeting (1:1-4) is the longest in the Pastorals and states the letter's themes in advance: truth and godliness, eternal life, God's word made public, God "our Savior". The body opens with a contrast built on repeated words: the elder is not "greedy for shameful profit" (1:7), the opponents teach "for the sake of shameful profit" (1:11); the elder can "correct" (1:9), and Titus must "correct them sharply" (1:13); God "does not lie" (1:2), and the Cretans are "always liars" (1:12).
views.J: "Those from the circumcision" (1:10), "Jewish myths" (1:14), purity rules (1:15) and genealogies (3:9) suggest teachers who drew on Jewish tradition. The letter's answer, that all things are clean to the clean, stands with Mark 7:19 and Romans 14:20. Jewish readers note that these were disputes among believers in Jesus over how much of Jewish practice Gentile believers should take on, as in Galatians and Acts 15, and that the verses have often been read as a judgment on Judaism itself, which they are not.
views.T: The chapter is a main text for church order. Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican readers see Titus as an apostolic delegate who ordains elders, a pattern of the bishop; Lutheran, Reformed and Baptist readers stress that "elder" and "overseer" name one office here (1:5, 7). "The husband of one wife" (1:6) has been read as forbidding a second marriage for clergy (so Chrysostom), as requiring fidelity, and in other ways (see the note). The card below sets out the readings of church order.

deep.h: Titus 1:5-9 and 1 Timothy 3:1-7: two lists compared
deep.b: The two lists of qualities for an overseer share much: "the husband of one wife", "sensible", "welcoming to strangers", "not a heavy drinker, not a man who hits people", and a concern for the man's children. But they differ in ways that fit their settings. Titus speaks of elders and the overseer in one breath (1:5, 7); 1 Timothy 3 speaks of the overseer and then of deacons, and treats elders later (1 Timothy 5:17). Titus calls the overseer "God's household manager" and asks for qualities 1 Timothy does not list: "not stubborn", "not hot-tempered", "love what is good", "righteous", "devout", "self-controlled", and a tight grip on "the word that can be trusted" with the ability to correct opponents (1:9). 1 Timothy 3 asks for things Titus does not: "able to teach", "not a recent convert", "a good name with outsiders", and two qualities, "forbearing" and "not a fighter", that Titus 3:2 asks of every believer. The missing "not a recent convert" fits a young church on Crete, where every candidate was new; in Ephesus, where the church was older, the rule could be kept. The two lists are close enough to share a source in common teaching, and different enough to show that each was shaped for a place.

The line in 1:12 has been quoted for two thousand years. Its words, "Cretans are always liars", are also in Callimachus' Hymn to Zeus (third century BC), where the poet calls the Cretans liars because they showed a tomb of Zeus, "but thou didst not die, for thou art for ever." Clement of Alexandria (Stromata 1.14) names Epimenides of Crete as the man Paul means, and the English of Chrysostom's third homily on Titus says the same; Calvin had "no doubt" of it. Koskenniemi argues that the saying began as a proverb, that a logical paradox grew around it, and that Epimenides was tied to it only later: no ancient source names a book of his that held the line until Jerome. Later logicians named the "liar paradox" after him: if a Cretan says all Cretans lie, is he telling the truth? The letter has a plainer aim. God "does not lie" (1:2), the opponents lead minds astray (1:10), and a Cretan's own words are brought against them. Readers differ on whether the line targets the false teachers or the Cretans as a people (see the note on 1:12); either way, the stated goal of the rebuke is "so that their faith will be sound" (1:13).

echoes: Acts 2:11; Acts 14:23; Acts 20:17-28; Acts 27:7-21; Acts 17:28; Galatians 2:1-5; Galatians 2:12; 2 Corinthians 7:6-15; 2 Corinthians 8:16-23; 1 Timothy 3:1-7; 1 Timothy 1:3-11; Mark 7:1-23; Romans 14:14-20; Numbers 23:19; Isaiah 29:13

settings.by: Paul, as the letter presents him
settings.to: Titus, Paul's Greek coworker, left to lead the churches of Crete; and through him the believers of the island's house churches, who would hear it read (the closing grace in 3:15 is to "all of you")
settings.when: after a stay on Crete that Acts does not record, while Paul is free and travelling, before a winter at Nicopolis (3:12)
settings.why: to give Titus Paul's full authority before the churches. The long opening ties Paul's commission to God's ancient promise and to "godliness", so that everything that follows, the elders, the households, the warnings, is heard as part of God's saving plan and not as Titus' own rules.
views: Paul writes to a coworker on a new field and expects the letter to be read to the churches to back him up.
A later follower writes in Paul's voice to churches of his own time, using Titus as the model of a faithful leader; the greeting presents Paul's teaching as the standard.

settings.to: Titus, who must appoint the elders; and the churches, who must accept the men he chooses
settings.when: for a young church on Crete, with believers in many towns and no settled leaders
settings.why: to give each town's believers leaders who would hold firmly to sound teaching and could answer the false teachers. The qualities bind the men chosen as elders, and they bind Titus in his choosing. Knowing that the opponents were greedy and divisive (1:10-11) explains why money, temper and household order take up most of the list.
views: Some read the list as advice for Crete's situation, a model to be adapted by each church.
Many churches have treated it, with 1 Timothy 3, as the standard for all ministers.

settings.to: Titus, and the believers in Crete who were hearing these teachers in their homes
settings.when: while the teachers were active and winning households
settings.why: to show Titus who the opponents were and how to respond: stop them by correction, not ignore them. The Cretan proverb and the sharp words were meant to wake up believers who were being drawn in, and to bring the teachers back to a sound faith (1:13).

traditions.q: Titus appoints elders by Paul's order (1:5), and the elders are called "the overseer" (1:7). Is Titus a bishop over presbyters, and are bishops a separate order?
views: The apostles had helpers and "appointed such men" to carry on their ministry, and "bishops by divine institution have succeeded to the place of the apostles" (Lumen Gentium 20); presbyters are the bishops' "prudent cooperators" (Lumen Gentium 28). Tradition, recorded by Eusebius, names Titus as the first to oversee the churches of Crete.

Timothy and Titus were bishops of Ephesus and Crete, given the right to ordain presbyters, as Titus 1:5 shows. That "bishop" and "presbyter" are not always distinguished in the apostolic writings shows only that the words were not yet as fixed as they later became (Pomazansky, Orthodox Dogmatic Theology).
The Preface to the Ordinal holds that "from the Apostles' time" there have been three orders of ministers, "Bishops, Priests, and Deacons".

The Treatise on the Power and Primacy of the Pope (1537, paragraphs 62-63) cites Jerome on Titus 1:5-7: all who preside over churches are both bishops and elders, and so "it is by human authority that the grades of bishop and elder or pastor are distinct". Ordination alone later set bishops apart (paragraph 64).
Calvin held that this passage "plainly shows that there is no distinction between a presbyter and a bishop", and that Titus did not choose elders alone but presided "as moderator, at the elections".

A church has two scriptural offices, "pastor/elder/overseer and deacon", and "the office of pastor/elder/overseer is limited to men as qualified by Scripture" (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article VI). Each congregation chooses its own leaders.

title: Sound Teaching for Every Household
sum: Titus is to teach what fits sound teaching, group by group. Older men are to be clear-headed and sound in faith, love and endurance. Older women are to carry themselves as if in holy service and to teach the younger women good sense, love for husband and children, work in the home and submission to their husbands, "so that the word of God is not insulted." The younger men are to be sensible, and Titus is to be their pattern. Slaves are to serve honestly, so that they "make the teaching of God our Savior beautiful."

The reason for all of it comes in 2:11-14, one of the letter's two great summaries. God's grace has appeared, with salvation for all people. It trains believers to deny ungodliness and live sensibly now, while they wait for "the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ", who gave himself to redeem them and make them his own people, eager for good works.
readings: Read as a code of conduct
The chapter sets out how each group in a household should live, much as Greek writers on household management did. Read this way, its rules describe a Christian order of home and church.

Three purpose clauses face outward (2:5, 8, 10): so that God's word is not insulted, so that opponents have nothing to say, so that the teaching looks beautiful. Read this way, the rules aim at a good name among outsiders in a particular society, and their form may change where that society's expectations change.
The household duties are framed by grace. Believers do not earn salvation by good behavior; grace "trains" them to it, and Christ died to make a people "eager for good works".

views.H: Roman households held husband, wife, children, slaves and freed dependents, and a house church met in such a home. Marriages were usually arranged by families, and running a household was serious work. Slaves could manage money and goods. Outsiders judged new religions by whether they upset this order. The "sensible" virtue (sophrosyne) was a classic Greek virtue, praised in men and women alike.
views.C: Critical scholars see in 2:1-10 a church settling into its society, adopting the household ethics of its neighbors, and some see a contrast with the freedom of Galatians 3:28. Others answer that Paul already gave household advice (1 Corinthians 7; Colossians 3:18-4:1) and that the outward-looking reasons here show a mission concern, not a retreat. The phrase "our great God and Savior" (2:13) is weighed with Romans 9:5 and 2 Peter 1:1 as evidence for early belief in Jesus as God.
views.L: The chapter has two parts: instructions (2:1-10) and their ground (2:11-14), framed by commands to Titus to speak (2:1, 15). Key words repeat: "sound" (2:1, 2, 8), "sensible" in five forms (2:2, 4, 5, 6, 12), "submit" (2:5, 9), "good works" (2:7, 14). The two verbs of appearing (2:11, 13) mark the Christian life as the time between two epiphanies.
views.J: Titus 2:14 builds on Israel's Scriptures: the redemption "from all lawless deeds" of the Greek Psalm 130:8, the cleansing and "they will be my people" of Ezekiel 37:23, and the "own private treasure" of Exodus 19:5 and Deuteronomy 7:6. These were promises to Israel. Jewish readers ask what it means for Gentile believers to take them up; Christian readers answer in several ways (see the topic church and Israel).
views.T: 2:4-5 is part of the debate over the roles of women and men, and 2:9-10 belongs to the long history of how the churches read the slavery passages. 2:13 was used against Arius in the fourth century and is read differently by Jehovah's Witnesses today. The cards below set out the readings of 2:4-5 and 2:13; for the wider questions see the cards at Ephesians 5 (headship), Ephesians 6 and Philemon 1:15-16 (slavery), and 1 Timothy 2 (women teaching).

deep.h: "Our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ": one person or two?
deep.b:
The Greek of 2:13 is tēs doxēs tou megalou theou kai sōtēros hēmōn Iēsou Christou: "of the glory of the great God and Savior of us, Jesus Christ." One article, "the" (tou), stands before "great God", and none before "Savior." J. Christopher Edwards (Tyndale Bulletin, 2011) sets out three main readings.

One person, Jesus Christ. In 1798 Granville Sharp published Remarks on the Uses of the Definitive Article in the Greek Text of the New Testament, arguing that when one article governs two singular nouns describing persons, joined by "and", both refer to the same person. On that rule "God" and "Savior" are one figure, and the name that follows tells who he is: Jesus Christ is "our great God and Savior". Daniel Wallace (Granville Sharp's Canon and Its Kin, 2009) has made what Edwards calls "the strongest case" for this reading, and Edwards names Murray Harris, George Knight and Jerome Quinn among others who hold it. In favor: elsewhere in the Pastorals the "appearing" is always Christ's (1 Timothy 6:14; 2 Timothy 4:1, 8). Clement of Alexandria, in his Exhortation to the Greeks, quotes 2:11-13 right after saying that the Word has "appeared as man, He alone being both, both God and man".

One figure, God, whose glory is Jesus Christ. Edwards reports a second view, held by Gordon Fee and Philip Towner: Sharp's rule holds, but "our great God and Savior" is God, and "Jesus Christ" stands beside "the glory": Christ is the glory of God that will appear. Wallace answers that six Greek words stand between "glory" and "Jesus Christ", too far apart to go together.

Two persons. Others read "the great God" as the Father and "our Savior Jesus Christ" as the Son, so that the rule does not apply. Edwards calls this view "the present minority" and names Martin Dibelius and Hans Conzelmann and Larry Hurtado among those who hold it. He argues for a form of it himself: 2:11-14 runs closely parallel to 1 Timothy 2:1-7, where the same writer says "God is one, and one also is the mediator between God and humans: Christ Jesus" (1 Timothy 2:5), so he would keep God and Christ apart here too. The King James Version ("the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ") allows two persons, and the New World Translation reads two (see the card below).

The history. Calvin reports that the Arians used the two-person reading to argue that the Son is less than the Father, and that "the orthodox teachers of the Church" claimed both titles for Christ. Calvin himself answered that the glory of the great God would be revealed "in his person", in Christ. Chrysostom, preaching on this verse, asked, "Where are those who say that the Son is inferior to the Father?"

What the Plain does. The Greek order is "the great God and Savior of us". The Plain moves "our" to the front, "our great God and Savior", so that "our" covers both nouns as the single article does. That is a choice: it follows Sharp's rule and treats "God" and "Savior" as one figure. The comma before "Jesus Christ" then names that figure, as Wallace reads it. On the two-person reading the line would run "the great God and our Savior, Jesus Christ".

deep.title: Claude's theory: "our Savior" is passed back and forth on purpose
deep.b: Titus uses "our Savior" six times in three pairs, each time first of God and then, within a few verses, of Jesus: 1:3 and 1:4; 2:10 and 2:13; 3:4 and 3:6. The pattern looks deliberate. If so, 2:13 is the hinge of the middle pair: "God our Savior" (2:10) is followed by "our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ" (2:13), which uses both words of one figure. The three pairs would then teach, by placement rather than argument, what 3:4-6 shows outright: the saving act of God is done through Jesus Christ, and the title belongs to both. This overlaps with commentators who note the shared title; the claim that the pairing is a planned structure is my own. The evidence is limited: the pairs could simply follow from the writer's habit of using the title often.

echoes: Ephesians 5:21-6:9; Colossians 3:18-4:1; 1 Peter 2:18-3:7; 1 Timothy 5:1-2; 1 Timothy 6:1-2; Romans 2:24; Mark 10:45; Galatians 1:4; Psalm 130:8; Ezekiel 37:23; Exodus 19:5; Deuteronomy 7:6; Deuteronomy 14:2; 1 Peter 2:9; 2 Peter 1:1; Romans 9:5; 1 Timothy 6:14

settings.what: Duties for each group in the household
settings.to: Titus, who is to teach them; the letter is written to him, and the older men, older women, young women, young men and slaves of the Cretan house churches hear these lines second hand, read aloud in the church or passed on through Titus and the older women (2:3-4). Many of them lived in households headed by unbelievers.
settings.when: while false teachers were unsettling households (1:11)
settings.why: to steady the households the false teachers were upsetting, and to give outsiders no reason to scorn the gospel. Each group's duties bind that group; the purposes (2:5, 8, 10) show that the readers were being watched by neighbors who judged them by the order of their homes. Knowing that, readers can see why wives' submission and slaves' honesty are tied to the good name of "the word of God".
views: Many churches read these duties as God's design for home and church in every age.
Many others read them as wise conduct in the Roman household, whose aim (a good witness) may call for different conduct elsewhere.

settings.what: The grace that has appeared: the ground of the duties
settings.when: as the reason for the household instructions
settings.why: to show that the conduct just described is not a moral code for its own sake but the life grace trains people for, between Christ's first coming and his appearing in glory. For believers who had been slaves of desires (3:3), and for slaves in the literal sense, it said that they belonged to a Redeemer who made them "his own private treasure".

traditions.q: Does 2:4-5 ("submitting to their own husbands", "so that the word of God is not insulted") set a lasting rule for wives?
views: Pius XI taught an "order of love" that includes "the primacy of the husband with regard to the wife and children, the ready subjection of the wife and her willing obedience", and added that this subjection "in its degree and manner may vary according to the different conditions of persons, place and time" (Casti Connubii 26, 28). John Paul II kept the husband as "head", in order to give himself up for his wife, but taught that in marriage the "subjection" is "not one-sided but mutual" (Mulieris Dignitatem 24).

Chrysostom, preaching on this verse, called a loving marriage the chief good of a household, "where the head is in harmony with the body", and read the reason given as Paul's concern "for the preaching of the word": a believing wife of an unbeliever who lives well brings the gospel glory, and may win her husband (Homilies on Titus 4).

Luther's Small Catechism, in its Table of Duties, gives wives Ephesians 5:22 and 1 Peter 3:6, on submitting to their own husbands as to the Lord, and husbands 1 Peter 3:7 with the line from Colossians 3, "be not bitter against them".

Calvin read 2:5 as calling wives to be "subject to the dominion of their husbands", and took the reason more widely than marriages to unbelievers: Paul demands "such strictness of life as not to bring the gospel into the contempt of the public".

The 1662 Book of Common Prayer asks the bride, "Wilt thou obey him, and serve him", and reads the wives' texts of Ephesians, Colossians and 1 Peter. In the Church of England's Common Worship marriage service the vows are the same for both, "to love and to cherish", with no promise to obey.

"A wife is to submit herself graciously to the servant leadership of her husband", and she has "the God-given responsibility to respect her husband and to serve as his helper in managing the household" (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article XVIII).

Divided. The Danvers Statement (1987) cites Titus 2:3-5 when it asks wives to "grow in willing, joyful submission to their husbands' leadership". Christians for Biblical Equality's statement holds that husbands and wives are bound in "mutual submission" and that the husband's role as "head" means "self-giving love and service".
Yes. Chrysostom, preaching on the verse, asked, "Where are those who say that the Son is inferior to the Father?", and said that "great" is said of God "not comparatively but absolutely".

Calvin noted that the Arians used the verse to set the Father as "the great God" above the Son, and answered that Paul joined Christ's name to "the great God" to teach that the glory of God will be revealed in Christ's person.

No. The New World Translation (2013) reads "the great God and of our Savior, Jesus Christ", two persons. Its study note grants that some scholars read one person and take the verse as proof that Scripture calls Jesus "the great God", but says that "many scholars and Bible translators" accept a rendering "referring to two distinct persons".

title: Saved by Mercy, Devoted to Good Works
sum: Titus is to remind the believers to submit to rulers and authorities, to be ready for good work, to insult no one and to be gentle with everyone. The reason is their own past: "we too" were once foolish, enslaved to desires, hateful. But when the kindness of God our Savior and his love for humankind appeared, he saved us, not because of our works but in keeping with his mercy, through "the bath of new birth and the renewing by the Holy Spirit", poured out richly through Jesus Christ, so that, justified by grace, we would become heirs of eternal life.

"This saying is trustworthy." Titus is to insist on it, so that believers give themselves to good works, and to avoid foolish debates, genealogies and fights about the law. A divisive person gets two warnings and then is turned away. The letter ends with travel plans: Artemas or Tychicus will come to replace Titus, who is to join Paul at Nicopolis for the winter, and Zenas and Apollos are to be sent on with everything they need.
readings: Many readers hear 3:4-7 as words spoken to or about the newly baptized: once lost, now washed, renewed, poured with the Spirit, justified, heirs. On this reading the "bath of new birth" is baptism, and the passage is a summary of what happened to them.
Read as a summary of the gospel

Others read 3:4-7 as a compact statement of Paul's gospel for Gentile believers, where the washing is a picture of the Spirit's inner work: salvation by mercy, not works; justification by grace; the hope of life.

views.H: Crete was under Roman rule, and small religious groups that seemed to upset households or public order drew suspicion. Teaching believers to be good citizens (3:1-2) answered that. The travel plans of 3:12-13 show the network of Paul's coworkers: Tychicus from Asia (Acts 20:4), Apollos from Alexandria (Acts 18:24), and Artemas and Zenas, otherwise unknown. Nicopolis is most often identified with the city in Epirus that Octavian, the later Augustus, founded after his victory at Actium.
views.C: Critical scholars note that 3:4-7 uses Pauline words (works, mercy, justified by grace, heirs) in a new style, and some think the writer took over an existing baptismal hymn or creed, marked by "This saying is trustworthy" (3:8). Defenders of Paul see the same teaching as Romans and Ephesians in a short form. The personal notes in 3:12-15 are a main argument for some real Pauline material in the letter; on the critical view they give it the feel of a real letter.
views.L: The "once ... but when" movement (3:3-4) mirrors 2:11-14: the two epiphany passages frame the letter's teaching. 3:4-7 is a single long sentence in Greek, moving from God's kindness to the Spirit to justification to the hope of eternal life, which brings the letter back to its opening (1:2). The repeated "good works" (3:1, 8, 14) closes each section.
views.J: The Spirit "poured out" (3:6) echoes Joel 2:28, quoted at Pentecost (Acts 2:17). "Fights about the law" and "genealogies" (3:9) return to the Jewish-Christian teachers of 1:10-14. The washing and renewal recall the prophets' promise of cleansing water and a new spirit (Ezekiel 36:25-26).
views.T: 3:5 is a central text in the debate over baptism: Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and many Anglican readers see baptism itself as the washing of new birth; Reformed readers see a sign and seal of the Spirit's work; Baptists read the washing as the Spirit's inner work, pictured by baptism. 3:10 ("a person who causes splits", Greek hairetikos) became a key text for church discipline and gave English the word "heretic". 3:1 joins Romans 13 in the long debate on church and state.

deep.b: The passage reads like a short creed. God's kindness and love for humankind "appeared" (an epiphany, like grace in 2:11). He saved us, not by works but by mercy. The means is "the bath of new birth and the renewing by the Holy Spirit". The Spirit was "poured out" (as in Joel 2:28 and Acts 2:17) through Jesus Christ. The result is that we are "justified by that grace of his" and become "heirs" of eternal life (compare Romans 8:17, "If we are children, we are also heirs"). Every person of the Trinity is named: God our Savior, the Holy Spirit, Jesus Christ our Savior. The formula "This saying is trustworthy" (3:8) marks it as known teaching, and the move from "we were once" to "he saved us" fits teaching given at baptism. Three questions divide readers: whether the "bath" is baptism (Chrysostom and Calvin both say yes); whether "by the Holy Spirit" belongs to the bath as well as the renewing; and how the passage relates to Paul's "works of the law" in Romans and Galatians.

The word in 3:10, hairetikos, comes from hairesis, "choice, school, party". Acts uses hairesis neutrally for the Sadducees and Pharisees (Acts 5:17; 15:5) and, from opponents' lips, for the Christians (Acts 24:5). Paul uses it for factions (1 Corinthians 11:19; Galatians 5:20). Here the person is one who makes a faction. In later church Greek and Latin the word came to mean someone who holds a condemned doctrine, and English "heretic" comes from it. The text's procedure is pastoral: two warnings, then separation, because such a person "stands condemned by his own judgment". Matthew 18:15-17 has a similar sequence. Later churches built much heavier measures on this verse; the verse itself goes no further than turning the person away.

echoes: Romans 13:1-7; 1 Peter 2:13-17; Ephesians 2:1-10; Romans 3:24; Romans 8:17; Joel 2:28; Acts 2:17; Acts 2:33; Ezekiel 36:25-27; Matthew 19:28; John 3:5; Ephesians 5:26; 1 Timothy 1:15; 1 Timothy 1:4; Matthew 18:15-17; Acts 20:4; Acts 18:24-28; 2 Timothy 4:10-12

settings.what: Duties toward rulers and all people
settings.to: the believers of Crete, through Titus ("remind them")
settings.when: as the letter turns from the household to life in the wider town
settings.why: to make the believers good neighbors and law-abiding subjects of Roman rule, so that the gospel would not be blamed for disorder. The command binds every believer; it does not explain what to do if rulers command wrong, a question taken up elsewhere (Acts 5:29).

settings.what: The trustworthy saying: saved by mercy
settings.by: Paul, likely using words the churches already knew
settings.when: as the ground for gentleness toward outsiders
settings.why: to remind believers that they were once no better than the outsiders they now live among, and that they were saved by God's mercy, not their works. That memory makes them gentle. Titus must "speak firmly" about it so that it bears fruit in good works.
views: Many think the words of 3:4-7 were spoken at or about baptism.
Others see a confession of faith used in teaching or worship.

settings.what: What to avoid, and the divisive person
settings.when: with the false teachers of 1:10-16 still active
settings.why: to keep Titus from being drawn into endless debate, and to give a clear, limited process for dealing with a person who splits the church. It protected the church without long trials: two warnings, then separation.

settings.to: Titus, and "all of you" in the churches (3:15)
settings.when: as Paul plans to winter at Nicopolis
settings.why: to arrange Titus' replacement and his journey to Paul, and to ask the church to support Zenas and Apollos. The final instruction makes that hospitality a case of the good works the whole letter calls for.
views: Paul, free after the imprisonment of Acts 28, really plans to winter at Nicopolis and summons Titus; the names are his coworkers' movements at the time.
A later writer adds travel plans and names to give the letter the feel of a real one and to tie Titus' authority to Paul's own circle; some on this view think genuine notes of Paul were used here.

traditions.q: Is "the bath of new birth" (3:5) baptism itself, and does baptism give the new birth?
views: Baptism "is also called 'the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit'", citing Titus 3:5, "for it signifies and actually brings about the birth of water and the Spirit" (Catechism of the Catholic Church 1215).

Baptism is "a Sacrament, in which a man who believes ... is born again of the Holy Ghost to a life spiritual and holy" (Philaret, Longer Catechism 288); the catechism cites Titus 3:4-6 to show that the Holy Spirit is received "through the Sacraments" (250). Chrysostom told those about to be baptized that "this purification is called the laver of regeneration" and compared it to a potter remaking a fallen clay vessel.

It is not the water that does such great things but the word of God in and with the water, and the faith that trusts that word; without the word the water is plain water, with it a baptism and a washing of new life. Luther's Small Catechism (on Baptism) grounds this in Titus 3, "by the washing of regeneration and renewing of the Holy Ghost".
Baptism is "a sign of Regeneration or new Birth, whereby, as by an instrument, they that receive Baptism rightly are grafted into the Church" (Thirty-Nine Articles, article 27).

Baptism is "a sign and seal of the covenant of grace" and of regeneration (Westminster Confession 28.1); the grace promised is "really exhibited, and conferred, by the Holy Ghost", though not tied to the moment (28.6). Calvin had "no doubt" 3:5 alludes to baptism, but held that salvation is not "contained in the outward symbol of water".

Baptism is "the immersion of a believer in water" and "an act of obedience symbolizing the believer's faith" in the crucified and risen Savior (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article VII). Baptists commonly read the washing of 3:5 as the Spirit's inner work, which baptism pictures.
